paras: The beating of Black voters at the Memphis First ward polls took place on August 5, 1880, when a crowd at the First ward polling place in Memphis, Tennessee, attacked about twenty-five Black men during the Shelby County election. The only account, in the Memphis Public Ledger, blamed the men for trying to keep white voters from the ballot box and said no one was seriously injured, although the same page reported that a Black coal-yard worker, Dick Lyles, was left insensible in the street. Outside Memphis, reports of the election described it as peaceful and did not mention the fighting.

The August 5 election chose county officers, and its main contest was for sheriff, between P. R. Athey, the Democratic nominee, Edward Shaw, a Black Republican, and John Powell of the Greenback party. White papers had treated Shaw's candidacy as a danger to the city; days before the vote the Dallas Daily Herald called him "a copper-colored, insolent, incendiary negro" and concluded that "Memphis is to be pitied." Athey won, with about 5,600 votes in the city to Shaw's 2,300, according to the wire report.

The Public Ledger's police column said the "bloody first" was "a little too warm to be healthy" for a while on election day: a vote was challenged, a knockdown followed, and a general melee ensued. Police Captain O'Haver had his clothing spattered with blood and knocked down and dragged out "two or three rowdies" before a relief arrived from the station house and the trouble calmed.

A separate item in the same issue said that about twenty-five Black men "had heads put on them" at the First ward polls. By the paper's account, the men made up a majority of the crowd and tried to keep white voters from the ballot box "by crowding the gangway." O'Haver and two policemen warned "the negroes" that a riot would occur unless they desisted, and about three in the afternoon "the crowd turned loose" on them. The attackers were not named, and their race was conveyed only by the item's contrast between the Black men and the white voters they were said to be blocking.

The Ledger reported that no one was seriously injured and that the result was only "a few bloody noses and sore heads." Under the heading "One of the Victims," however, it reported that Dick Lyles, who worked in a coal yard, came out of the First ward row "badly beaten over the head," staggered several squares to Johnson avenue, and fell in the street insensible a few steps from his house. He was carried home and was reported considerably improved the next morning.

No report of any arrest of the attackers appears in the coverage. The same police column instead recorded charges of illegal voting against two men, Wyatt Gramlin, described as colored, who was discharged when no one appeared to prosecute, and Alex Samford.

The fighting at the First ward polls appears only in the Memphis Public Ledger, in short local items written from the side of the crowd. The paper described the beaten men as "obstreperous, bulldozing darkies" and said the crowd "cleaned them out beautifully."

Elsewhere the election reached readers through a Memphis wire dispatch, printed in Minnesota, Delaware and Pennsylvania, that gave only the returns. A Cincinnati Commercial special reprinted in Richmond called it the most exciting election in thirty years and said it ended "in the triumph OF peace and or der" [order]. Later Republican criticism, summarized in a New Haven editorial, attacked the count in the First ward, where returns exceeded the number of voting-age men by 322, but said nothing of violence at the polls. No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.

The Public Ledger gave two causes for the First ward fighting: its police column traced it to a challenged vote and a knockdown, while its longer item blamed Black men for crowding the gangway to the ballot box. Both versions come from the same paper, and no account from the men who were beaten appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Beating of Black voters at the Memphis First ward polls
bases: A crowd at the First ward polls attacked and beat about twenty-five Black men during the Memphis county election, injuring at least one badly, with no killing reported (A8, A7, A6).
All reports of the beating come from items in one issue of the Memphis Public Ledger (A5, A6, A7, A8); wire reports of the election (A2, A9) do not mention it.

accounts.label: Memphis Public Ledger, First ward item
accounts.gist: About twenty-five Black men, a majority of the crowd, crowded the gangway to keep white voters from the ballot box; after police warnings the crowd attacked them about 3 p.m.; no one seriously hurt.

accounts.label: Memphis Public Ledger, police column
accounts.gist: A challenged vote led to a knockdown and a general melee in the 'bloody first'; Captain O'Haver fought his way through and a relief calmed it, leaving bloody noses and black eyes.

accounts.label: Memphis Public Ledger, 'One of the Victims'
accounts.gist: Dick Lyles was badly beaten over the head in the First ward row and collapsed insensible near his home.

accounts.label: Wire and correspondent reports of the election
accounts.gist: Gave the vote and described the election as ending in peace and order, without mention of fighting.

framing.detail: The Ledger blamed the Black men for blocking white voters, called them 'obstreperous, bulldozing darkies', and said the crowd 'cleaned them out beautifully'.
Wire dispatches reported only the returns, and a Cincinnati Commercial special called it 'the triumph of peace and order'.
A Republican-leaning New Haven editorial attacked the Shelby County count as fraudulent but did not mention violence.
